Work with us

Work with us

An early, unfinished proposal. It needs people who can find what is wrong with it and build what is missing.

Written 19 October 2026, from the project's own notes and the app as it stood that day.

Triarchal Democracy is an early, unfinished proposal for how a community could decide things together. The founding documents are first drafts and the software has gaps that are listed in public. The project needs two kinds of people: those who can find what is wrong with it, and those who can build what is missing.

If that is you, this page says where to start. It lists real open problems, grouped by the kind of help they need, and each one points to the clause or the Known limits entry it comes from. It is not a job advertisement. Nothing here is paid, and the section on how contributions are recorded says exactly what you would get instead.

  • Software engineers
  • Legal and policy people
  • Researchers and economists
  • Designers, writers and organisers
  • How contributions are recorded
  • How to reach us
Software engineers

Identity, the ledger, security and the app

The Triarc runs on Triarchal Framework, a web application built with Hono on Cloudflare Workers, with a D1 database. It is licensed under the GNU Affero General Public License, version 3, and the licence file ships with the project. A licence says what you may do with the code once you have it; it does not put the code anywhere you can browse. If you want to read the code, say so when you introduce yourself (see below) and the project will share it with you.

Open problems.

  • Verify the randomness beacon's signature. Dispute Panels are drawn from a round of the public drand "quicknet" beacon. The software re-runs the shuffle but does not check the beacon's own signature, so a false value fed to it would produce a draw that re-runs cleanly. (Dispute Procedure Code 3.1; Known limits)
  • Design the identity and ledger stages the Charter commits to. Identity is a password and a phone number today; the Charter commits to cryptographic integrity proofs, then privacy-preserving mechanisms, then a zero-knowledge design. The record is append-only by convention; the Charter commits to integrity proofs anchoring each entry and then a chained public ledger. None of it is under way, and the first job is a scoping pass: what to prove, where to anchor it, at what cost, and without any Member needing a wallet. (Charter 1.5, 7.1; Treasury Code 6.4; identity, ledger)
  • Choose and connect a notification provider. Preferences are stored and an in-app inbox covers a few kinds of event, but no email is sent. The most serious consequence is that a Member drawn for a Dispute Panel is not told, though they have 48 hours to decline. The design has to respect two rules: no push channel, because the app runs no client-side JavaScript, and no manufactured urgency. (Rules of Procedure 4.3; Known limits)
  • Close the entrenchment gap. The software applies the Charter's three-quarters rule when a proposal names the protected clause it amends. A proposal that describes its change only in free text is not content-checked. No fix has been chosen, and the hard part is design: how to check what a proposal really amends without a person deciding for everyone else. (Charter 8.2; Known limits)
  • An independent security review. The dependency checker reports known vulnerabilities in some packages, mostly development tooling, and nobody has gone through them one by one. Every review so far was run by the project itself. A reviewer might start with sign-in and sessions, the phone-verification flow, the rate limits and the discipline that keeps the record append-only. (Known limits)
  • Resist sign-up abuse without turning people away. Sign-ups are capped per network and across the community, and a spike can make real people wait. A stronger defence than caps has not been added. (Known limits, accounts)
  • Smaller gaps. A download of the public record that anyone could keep a copy of; a dashboard line for concentrated delegation holders and a notice to delegators whose delegations end; recovery of dividends paid on a contribution later voided. (Hard questions; Known limits; Code of Conduct 3.4)

A first small contribution

You do not need the code for this. Pick one item above and write down how you would approach it: a one-page threat model of the sign-in and verification flow, built from the descriptions on Known limits and in the Triarc Membership Code, or a comparison of three email providers (cost per message, where the data is held, what the project would have to hand over). Post it as a discussion, as described under "How to reach us".

Legal and policy people

Nonprofit law, privacy law, and the weak points of the documents

No lawyer has reviewed any of the founding documents, and the Triarc is not incorporated. These are the questions the project cannot answer for itself.

Open problems.

  • The nonprofit structure. The plan is a federal corporation under the Canada Not-for-profit Corporations Act, with a two-layer design so that participants can receive a dividend while Delegates elect the directors. Whether that design avoids the rules on what a nonprofit may distribute to its own members is untested. (Federation Compact Article VIII, 8.4; Triarc Membership Code 4.1; Known limits)
  • The age rule. Anyone aged eighteen or older may join by declaring their age, and nothing checks it. Where the age of majority is above eighteen, a Member who has declared eighteen is entitled to the dividend before reaching it. The founder intends to seek legal advice on that, and the question is not yet answered. (Charter 1.1; Known limits)
  • An accountable operator, terms of use and a privacy policy. The software has none of the three yet, and who the accountable operator is has not been settled. (Hard questions; Known limits)
  • Tax treatment of the dividend. Whether either dividend tier would be taxable for the people who receive it is a question for counsel, not yet put or answered. (Known limits)
  • A permanent public record against privacy law. The record keeps a username and everything done under it, even after an account is closed. How that sits with laws that give a right to erasure has not been reviewed by a lawyer. (Charter 1.3, 7.1; Hard questions)
  • Red-team the Charter and the Codes. Governance scholars are asked to find the route to capture the authors missed. The authors already know three soft spots: the criteria that end the founder's powers measure activity, not independence, and one operator running many accounts could in principle produce all of it; the core protections are guarded by a three-quarters rule that the software applies only when a proposal names the clause it changes; and every default is a stated judgement, not a finding. (Charter 2.6, 8.2, Article IX)

A first small contribution

Pick one clause, read it as an opponent would, and write a page: what it permits that it should not, and what you would change. Or read the Member Bill of Rights and say which of its ten rights could not be enforced in practice, and why.

Researchers and economists

Voting theory, delegation, the dividend and what to measure

The Triarc says its main output is evidence, including evidence of failure. It intends to publish measures such as delegation-renewal rates, Dispute Panel outcomes and treasury arithmetic on a fixed cadence (About The Triarc). Most of the numbers that would be measured were chosen by judgement, and the people best placed to test them are not on the project.

Open problems.

  • Simulate delegation concentration. The rule that is meant to stop permanent super-delegates triggers at ten supporters and 10% of a sector's delegation, with a confirmation vote at 20%. Those thresholds are chosen, not derived, and the rule has never met real behaviour. How does concentration grow under different network models, and where do the thresholds start to punish trusted people in small sectors? (Charter 2.6, 3.6; Known limits)
  • Gaming by splitting. If holdings are split across accounts to stay under a threshold, the rule cannot tell. How much does that weaken it, and what would detect it? (Known limits)
  • Check the dividend arithmetic. Full distribution of a cycle needs about one Member in nine to be contributing, once both tiers are counted against the five-times cap, and the residue the cap holds back carries into the next Foundation Dividend. The costing model on the arithmetic page rests on one assumption it labels as an assumption: how much public payroll citizen deliberation could stand in for. Read both adversarially. (Charter 5.3, 5.3a; Treasury Code 4.3; The arithmetic)
  • The thinnest numbers. The 30-Member activation gate is the most consequential chosen number in the documents, and it cannot be amended away once it has opened. Domain weights, the 90-day Active window and the Phase criteria are judgements too. Which would you test first, and with what data? (Treasury Code 5.1a; Contribution Code 2.1; Charter 2.6)
  • Voting rules at small scale. Thresholds, participation floors and windows were reasoned for a community of a few dozen Members at founding. How do they behave there, and as it grows? (Rules of Procedure 1.3, 1.3b; Charter 3.5a)
  • Measurement design. What would be a good measure of independence, as opposed to activity? How do you publish governance data on a small community without exposing individuals? What would show that contribution is reaching people with little free time, which is the question the Contribution Code says its review must ask? (Contribution Code 6.2; Charter 2.6)

A first small contribution

Choose one chosen number, say what data would test it, and say what result would make you move it. Or write a short, reproducible simulation of delegation chains with your assumptions stated, and post the method and the result.

Designers, writers and organisers

Usability, translation, explanation and community practice

A governance system that only fluent, online, English-speaking people can use will count only them. The proposition says the system must work on an inexpensive phone over a slow connection, in the languages the community speaks. That is a requirement still to be tested.

Open problems.

  • Usability and accessibility testing. The app has been checked for accessibility only by reading its code, in the project's own review. Nobody has watched a newcomer use it, or tested it with a screen reader, with keyboard-only navigation or on a slow phone. (The proposition)
  • French translation. The site, the app and the documents are in English only. The Contribution Code counts translation as Craft. Translation of the plain-language pages and the Member Bill of Rights would be a useful first piece, labelled with the version translated. (Charter 2.2; Contribution Code, Section 2)
  • Explainer design. There is no explainer video and no walk-through of how a vote moves along a delegation chain.
  • Hard questions we did not ask. The Hard questions page answers eleven. Which twelfth would a sceptic ask?
  • Community moderation practice. The Code of Conduct and the Dispute Panel system are built but have never been used by real Members. In the first phase the founder may appoint interim moderators, a panel cannot be drawn until at least 30 volunteers are in the pool, and the Triarc defines no moderation sector. Where would a real moderator get stuck? How would you recruit and look after a volunteer pool? (Charter 9.2; Dispute Procedure Code 2.1; Known limits)

A first small contribution

Join, spend your first half hour as a stranger, and write down every place you were unsure what to do next. Or translate one short page. Or write the twelfth hard question and a draft answer.

Credit and money

How contributions are recorded

Under the Contribution Code you log what you did, with evidence such as a link to the work. The entry starts as pending. It is verified once at least two Active Members who did not collaborate on it attest to it, and you then have 60 days to claim it for it to count. (Contribution Code 1.4, 3.1, 3.3) The Charter makes the Contribution Record a public, permanent, append-only ledger. (Charter 2.1) In the app today the full ledger page is for signed-in Members, and each logged contribution also appears as a line on the public Record. Credit here means that: a public record, under your username, of what you did. A username is a handle, not your name.

One honest limit: verification needs other Members. While few people are here, an entry can wait for attestations that nobody is yet around to give.

No payment

No payment, salary, equity or income is offered or promised. Nothing here is a job, a contract or a promise of a role. The Foundation Dividend is gated and not live: a gate in the software holds both dividend tiers until a deployment has 30 verified Members and every Delegate Position it has defined is filled, and nothing has been paid to anyone. (Treasury Code 5.1) The amount is "never fixed or promised in advance". (Treasury Code 5.3)

The Contribution Marks you accrue are a record. Whether they would ever count towards money depends on a gate that has not opened and on a treasury that does not yet hold the money. Please do not contribute for that reason. Contribution never changes the weight of anyone's vote. (Charter 2.5)

The documents let a community budget compensation for the Delegates it elects to Positions. (Charter 4.3; Treasury Code 3.2) That is something the community decides by vote, not something this page offers, and nothing has been paid to anyone.

First contact

How to reach us

There is no email address, no contact form and no private messaging, and for now that is deliberate: the Charter says nothing that binds the community may happen off the record. (Charter 7.3) First contact is therefore public, through an account on the Triarc itself. Here is the path, step by step.

  1. Register. The form asks for a username (3 to 20 letters, numbers, underscores or hyphens), an email address (kept private, used to sign in), a password of at least 8 characters, and a tick-box saying you are at least 18. The phone field is optional; leave it blank. Your username is public and stays on the record for good, so do not use your legal name unless you want it there. (Charter 1.1, 7.2) If sign-ups are briefly paused, the app's status page says so, and it lifts by itself.
  2. Follow a sector. After you register the app asks which sectors you want to follow. The Triarc has three: Data Collection & Research, Nonprofit Operations and Software Stewardship. (Triarc Operations Code 2.1) Engineers will want Software Stewardship, researchers Data Collection & Research, and legal, policy, design, writing and organising people Nonprofit Operations. Following is a self-declared interest and costs nothing. (Contribution Code 2.4)
  3. Introduce yourself in that sector's discussion. Open the Sectors tab, choose the sector, and use the "Start a discussion" box. Give it a title that says what you offer and which problem you would look at, and in the text say what you can do, which open problem above you have in mind, and, if you are an engineer, that you would like to read the code. A link to work you have published is welcome. The profile page has no free-text field, so this post is your introduction. Its title appears on the public Record, so keep personal details out of it.
  4. Optionally, post to the Opportunities board. It is meant for tasks the community needs done, so use it for a task you propose to do or want help with. Tag a sector: Members who follow that sector and have switched on the alert will see it in their in-app inbox.
  5. Or comment on a proposal, with or without an account. The Proposals page is public. A visitor may comment on any proposal without registering, under a lower-visibility identity: a display name of your choice or "a visitor". That comment is anonymous, earns no Marks and cannot be answered privately. A Member comments under their username. A comment that finds a flaw in an open proposal is a real contribution. If no proposal is listed, use step 3. (Rules of Procedure 2.4)
  6. Check back. Nothing is pushed to you. Notification email is not built, and a reply to your post does not trigger an in-app alert either, so come back to the discussion. No reply time is promised, and few people are here yet.
What does not work yet

Voting is not open yet. On the Triarc voting and delegating need a verified phone number, and the text-message service that sends the code is not connected. Registering, reading, commenting, proposing, posting and logging contributions do not wait for it. (Triarc Membership Code 2.1; Known limits) There is no private messaging, no contact address and no email notification, which is why first contact is public. Whatever you post, other Members can read, and the Record keeps a line about it.
